title: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI's Dots agents buy things — without seeing the card
subtitle: US Pro subscribers can delegate purchases to Dots behind a tokenized credential, with per-transaction approval and existing card rewards preserved.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on November 13, starting with US-based ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older who hold an eligible US-issued card. The feature plugs into Dots, OpenAI's always-on agent runtime, and lets a Dot complete purchases on a user's behalf after a one-time card entry and a per-transaction approval. OpenAI built the integration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.

The technical shape of the product is the news — not the convenience. Agents never receive the card number. Each purchase flows through a tokenized credential the card network issues, so merchants and the agent both see a short-lived token instead of the primary account number. A security check fires on every transaction, and OpenAI says users keep their existing card rewards and the consumer protections attached to the card. That architecture is what card networks insisted on before letting any AI system sit inside the payment flow.

OpenAI is pairing the launch with a Commerce Partner Playbook aimed at merchants, asking payment systems to recognise legitimate agent activity rather than block it as fraud. The company said it eventually plans to let users delegate purchases under preset conditions — spending limits, product categories, time windows — though those controls are not in the initial release. The announcement arrives two days after United Airlines amended its contract of carriage to prohibit AI agents from booking flights. The question of which merchants will route around agent traffic, and which will court it, is now a live commercial fight.

A takeaway for learners: Wallet is the first production example of an agent that can spend real money at scale. The design — tokenisation, per-transaction consent, no raw card exposure — is a template worth studying. When you build or evaluate an agent that takes an action in the world, the questions are usually the same: what can it see, what can it do without asking, and what happens if it goes wrong. Wallet answers all three in public, and that answer will become the reference point for whatever follows.
